newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey prepares first stage of Iranian gas deal.
newsitem.headline: Turkey prepares first stage of Iranian gas deal.

text.p: A Turkish pipeline company sought bids on Thursday for the construction of a 300-km (188-mile) pipeline to transport natural gas from Iran to Turkey in the first stage of a $23-billion deal with the Islamic Republic.

The 23-year accord, struck during a visit to Tehran in August by Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, sailed close to contravening a United States law aimed at discouraging third countries' investment in energy projects in Iran.
The project is vital to Turkey's long-term plans to meet domestic energy demand which is estimated to grow 12 percent annually, energy officials say.
"This project is very important to Turkey in view of its energy needs," Ugur Dogan, undersecretary at the Turkish energy ministry told Reuters.

Pipeline company Botas issued a tender statement in Turkey's Official Gazette on Thursday, seeking bids to build the stretch of pipeline between the eastern Turkish towns of Erzurum and Dogubeyazit, on the Iranian border.
Bids for construction of the 40-inch (100-cm) diameter pipeline are sought by February 28, 1997.

Dogan said the entire pipeline construction project in Turkey is estimated to cost around $1.1 billion, adding that the second stage would involve the extension of the pipeline from Erzurum to the Turkish capital Ankara, 800 km (500 miles) away.
"We may seek domestic or international credit for the construction of the second stage of the pipeline between Erzurum and Ankara," he said.
He said the pipeline will link up with a gas line to Russia, from which Turkey may increase gas imports by up to 16 billion cubic metres from about 6 billion a year currently.
There are also plans to extend the pipeline from Ankara to Europe for the distribution of natural gas there.
The pipeline to Iran will carry an initial three billion cubic metres of Iranian natural gas annually from 1999, to be raised to 10 billion cubic metres from 2005.
A 270-km (169-mile) pipeline is to be built from the Iranian town of Tabriz to the Turkish border to link up with the line from Dogubeyazit under the deal.

Iran and Turkey must each build the section of the pipeline through their territories to avoid breaching a U.S. decision in August that investors putting at least $40 million in energy projects in Iran and Libya would be punished.

Turkey's Erbakan reached agreement on the Iranian deal on a controversial visit to Tehran soon after he was elected. The trip was criticised by Ankara's NATO ally the United States, which has sought to isolate Iran internationally.
Turkey said on Wednesday it had discussed defence industry cooperation with a visiting Iranian official.
Under the gas agreement Iran will sell Turkey about 190 billion cubic metres of gas, to be mainly used for power generation along the line.
Faced with the prospect of growing energy deficits in the future, Turkey has already started importing electricity and plans the construction of nuclear, thermal and hydraulic plants.
A tender is expected to be issued next week for the construction of a nuclear power plant at Akkuyu, near the southern Turkish port of Mersin.
The plant, likely to cost around $1.5 billion, will have a capacity of 1,200 MegaWatts (MW), energy officials say.
Turkey has a power generation capacity of 105 billion kWh but production expectations stand at 93.1 billion kWh against expected consumption of 97.5 billion kWh.
